section_summary: Pages 1–31 are a continuation of the file’s chronological “List of Papers,” indexing 1938 diplomatic reports, congressional correspondence, public protests, petitions, and Department replies about exports of arms, scrap iron, oil, aircraft, and other strategic materials to Japan. Pages 32–62 contain the opening substantive correspondence: citizens and labor or church groups urge an embargo, while the State Department repeatedly explains that the Neutrality Act cannot prohibit scrap-iron or other raw-material exports and has not been invoked against either belligerent. The section also includes a naval attaché report on Japanese scrap purchases in Nicaragua, a union protest concerning a government-owned ship, reports of the Nanking atrocities, and petitions from Seattle churches.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Army Equipment—Japan, entries 171–452
subfiles.about: A chronological index summarizes diplomatic reports, citizen protests, petitions, congressional referrals, and replies concerning military and strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This continuation of the file index begins with entry 171 and records documents from early 1938 through November. Most entries concern demands that the United States stop exporting arms, airplanes, scrap iron, petroleum, cotton, trucks, and other materials useful to Japan's war in China. Department replies typically transmitted the Neutrality Act or related pamphlets and explained the absence of legal authority for a unilateral embargo. The index also identifies diplomatic reporting on Japanese procurement in Europe, Asia, and the Americas.

subfiles.title: Ludella W. Goodspeed protest against oil and iron exports
subfiles.about: Goodspeed asks the President to prevent oil and iron from being exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary Seattle protest by Ludella Goodspeed urging that oil and iron exports to Japan end; White House referral marks.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ludella W. Goodspeed
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department states that no existing statute authorizes the President to prohibit oil and iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says current statutes do not empower the President to prohibit oil and iron exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: C. A. Hayes letter and clipping on Japanese pig-iron purchases
subfiles.about: Hayes forwards a newspaper report alleging that Japan was buying American pig iron and industrial equipment for naval armament.
subfiles.summary: Hayes's protest on pig-iron exports with an AP clipping in which Upton Close predicts conflict and says Japanese battleship materials came from Birmingham and Pittsburgh.

subfiles.title: Reply to C. A. Hayes
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises Hayes that the President lacks statutory power to prohibit pig-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says no existing statute authorizes the President to prohibit pig-iron exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters request for an embargo
subfiles.from: C. R. Van Winkle, Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters
subfiles.about: The carpenters' council asks Roosevelt to support an embargo on war and potential war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters urges an embargo of war materials as peaceful pressure to halt Japanese aggression and advance peace and American security.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to C. R. Van Winkle
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why most raw-material exports could not legally be stopped.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends the May 1, 1937 resolution and proclamation: a war finding would bar arms to both China and Japan, no authority discriminates against Japan alone, and other materials cannot be prohibited; Roosevelt judged invocation against broader interests.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on Japanese purchases of Nicaraguan scrap iron
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.about: The report summarizes Nicaraguan press claims that local scrap iron was being bought for shipment to Japan and conversion into armaments.
subfiles.summary: Naval attaché: La Nueva Prensa says the old ship Momotombo was sold to Morris Pataky for resale as scrap to a Japanese firm; the Panama Canal Department reportedly sold scrap to Japanese buyers.

subfiles.title: National Maritime Union telegram protesting scrap-iron transport
subfiles.from: Fredrick Myers, National Maritime Union Committee
subfiles.about: Myers protests the use of a government-owned merchant ship to carry 5,000 tons of scrap iron from Brooklyn to Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: National Maritime Union says the City of Rayville loads scrap for Yokohama at Brooklyn Pier 16, violating the spirit of treaties; asks Hull to stop it.

subfiles.title: Reply to Fredrick Myers on scrap iron aboard government-owned vessels
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that scrap iron is not legally classified as an implement of war and may therefore be exported on government-owned merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Green says scrap iron is not among enumerated arms, so no restriction applies to exporting it to Japan, even on a government-owned vessel; encloses the President's September 14, 1937 statement.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Henry B. Twombly's letter
subfiles.about: Roosevelt asks the Secretary of State to reply to Henry B. Twombly's enclosed letter.
subfiles.summary: White House asks State to reply to Henry Twombly's letter at Roosevelt's request.

subfiles.title: Henry B. Twombly letter on the Nanking atrocities and American exports
subfiles.about: After hearing George Fitch's eyewitness account of Nanking, Twombly asks the President to stop American war materials from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Twombly, after hearing George Fitch on Nanking, compares Japanese atrocities to the sack of Magdeburg and asks Roosevelt to stop war-material supplies.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Henry B. Twombly
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act and supplies comparative arms-export licensing figures for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green says no authority exists to bar arms to Japan alone without a war finding; since July 1, 1937 the Department licensed $12,136,114.16 in arms to China and $5,907,658.28 to Japan.

subfiles.title: Henry B. Twombly acknowledgment
subfiles.about: Twombly thanks Green for the reply and notes approvingly that licensed arms exports to China exceeded those to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Twombly thanks Green, is satisfied more armament went to China, and condemns Japan's warfare.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on rayon-contaminated cotton waste
subfiles.about: The memorandum calls attention to a Kobe report that legally required rayon admixture made Japanese cotton-cloth waste unsuitable for ammunition manufacture.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern memo: Kobe despatch 238 notes rayon in Japanese cotton textiles made their waste poor for ammunition production.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hong Kong despatch on the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects researchers to a despatch about Japanese lead purchases and operation of the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hong Kong despatch 136 of March 16, 1938 on Japan's purchase of lead and the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner cover letter to the President
subfiles.about: Hiltner tells Roosevelt that he is sending Hull petitions from Seattle citizens protesting scrap-iron and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner sends the Secretary a packet with several hundred signatures, copying the covering letter and offering religious support to Roosevelt.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner letter transmitting Seattle church petitions
subfiles.about: Hiltner forwards church petitions and describes Seattle opposition to a recent scrap-iron shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner says Seattle church signatures were collected quickly, describes a scrap-laden ship and a silent picket, and says labor, church and business groups resent war-material exports.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Walter G. Hiltner
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the petitions and explains why neither scrap-iron exports nor arms exports to Japan alone could be prohibited under existing law.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the May 1, 1937 resolution and arms pamphlet: neutrality would bar arms to both sides, scrap iron is not an enumerated implement, no statute allows prohibiting scrap exports; Roosevelt judged invocation against broad interests.

subfiles.title: Department-routed copy of Walter G. Hiltner's petition letter
subfiles.about: A routed copy repeats Hiltner's submission of Seattle church petitions against scrap-iron and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department copy of Hiltner's petition letter with routing marks, describing the Seattle protest and humanitarian case.

subfiles.title: Green Lake United Presbyterian Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Green Lake United Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Church members appeal for legislation prohibiting scrap iron and munitions shipments to any aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: The printed petition asks all branches of the federal government to hasten legislation banning scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor states. Two pages contain signatures and Seattle addresses from members of the Green Lake United Presbyterian Church and its congregation.

subfiles.title: Sea View Methodist Protestant Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Sea View Methodist Protestant Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Sea View church members request legislation barring shipments of scrap iron and munitions to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Sea View Methodist Protestant Church petition, parallel to the Green Lake appeal, asking the government to prohibit scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressors.

subfiles.title: Petition of Seattle residents
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Seattle residents petition for legislation against scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Seattle residents' petition seeking federal legislation; signatures largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Sea View Methodist Protestant Church members and friends petition
subfiles.from: Members and friends of Sea View Methodist Protestant Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: A further Sea View petition asks for legislation prohibiting scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Another Sea View Methodist Protestant Church petition with a handwritten list of supporters and addresses.
